implementation_notes: The temporal collection collapses into an ordered associative container keyed by the effective start: std::map<std::chrono::sys_days, Value> with the lookup upper_bound(when) followed by one step back gives the version in force, and std::chrono::time_point/time_point_cast is the Time Point (sys_days makes the date granularity explicit in C++20). The owner keeps only the accessor pair (value(when) plus a current() that reads the clock once), and put() is insert_or_assign at an effective date. What replaces the classic structure: the container owns ordering and the bound search, so no Effectivity or TemporalCollection class is needed; the explicit range objects are still justified when validity is not a simple 'latest start <= date' - e.g. gaps, overlaps, or several values valid at once - or when the store must round-trip to a relational table.
pitfalls: std::prev(byStart_.begin()) is undefined behaviour: the check for 'no milestone at or before the date' must come first, and empty histories are the common case in tests.

sys_days is UTC-based while the business date is usually a local calendar day - converting with current_zone()/local_days and a fixed zone (not the ambient one) is required, or a change effective '1 January' lands on 31 December for half the world.

operator[] and insert_or_assign at an existing key silently discard the stored version, so a same-date correction (a second update on the same day) leaves no trace unless the key carries a revision or a second time dimension.

std::map nodes are stable but std::vector is not: if the milestone store is swapped for a vector + std::upper_bound (cheaper for short histories) any iterator or reference handed out by the accessor is invalidated by the next put().
